links.passage: Application efficiencies of microirrigation systems are typically high because these systems distribute water near or directly into the crop root zone; therefore, water losses resulting from wind drift and evaporation are typically small resulting in a highly efficient (90% to 95%) water delivery system (Boman, 2002).
reference_entries: Boman, B.J. 2002. Efficiency, uniformity, and system evaluation, p. 399–414. In: B.J. Boman (ed.). Water and Florida citrus: Use, regulation, systems, and management. Univ. Florida Inst. Food Agr. Sci. Press, Gainesville, FL.

links.passage: The advantages of microirrigation over sprinkler include: reduced water use, ability to apply fertilizer with the irrigation, precise water distribution, reduced foliar diseases, and the ability to electronically schedule irrigation on large areas with relatively smaller pumps.
supporting_passages: Application efficiencies of microirrigation systems are typically high because these systems distribute water near or directly into the crop root zone; therefore, water losses resulting from wind drift and evaporation are typically small resulting in a highly efficient (90% to 95%) water delivery system (Boman, 2002).
links.inference_note: The sentence listing reduced foliar diseases as an advantage of microirrigation immediately follows the sentence carrying the Boman (2002) citation on microirrigation efficiency.

links.passage: Less efficiency has been found for a microsprinkler system compared with a drip irrigation system.
supporting_passages: Application efficiencies of drip and line source systems are primarily dependent on hydraulics of design of these systems and on their maintenance and management (Boman, 2002; Boman and Parsons, 1993).
links.inference_note: The claim that drip is more efficient than microsprinkler is uncited, with the citation on drip application efficiencies sitting in the following sentence.

links.passage: Proper maintenance of a microirrigation system will extend system life, improve performance, minimize downtime, reduce the probability of nonuniform water and fertilizer applications resulting from emitter plugging, reduce operating costs, and save water and fertilizer (Boman, 1990, 1995).
reference_entries: Boman, B.J. 1990. Clogging characteristics of various microsprinkler designs in a mature citrus grove. Proc. Florida State Hort. Soc. 103:327–330.
Boman, B.J. 1995. Effect of orifice size on microsprinkler discharge rates. Appl. Eng. Agr. 11:839–843.

links.passage: Several field studies have determined the importance of proper irrigation scheduling on citrus growth and production on the low water-holding nutrient-retention soils of central Florida (Boman, 1994; Morgan et al., 2006a; Parsons et al., 2001; Scholberg et al., 2002).
supporting_passages: These methods are use of soil moisture sensors and/or crop ET.
Regardless of the methods used, the goals of providing optimum soil moisture for plant growth and productivity and reduction of fertilizer nutrient leaching are the same.
links.inference_note: The preceding sentences define the scheduling strategies as sensor- or crop-ET-based (data/model-driven) scheduling, and the cited sentence states their importance for citrus growth and production.
